extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal practitioners, and judges studying British copyright law (historical/principles)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the statutory foundations, constructions, and judicially-developed rules governing literary property (copyright) in the United Kingdom, including duration, scope, piracy, manuscripts, letters, and limits (obscenity/libel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory foundation of copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: All literary property or copyright is either founded by construction on the statute of 8 Anne, or given by the positive provisions of other acts of parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise identifies the statutes (e.g., 8 Anne c.19; 13 Geo. III c.50; 41 Geo. III c.107; 54 Geo. III c.156) as the legal basis for authors' rights. Subsequent acts consolidate and extend previous provisions; statutory text and recitals govern interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of copyright (statutory terms and renewals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 8 Anne an author's printed book had 14 years; unpublished works later enjoyed 14 years (then 28 years under later statute), with a further term of 14 years (or life residuum) if the author lived out the first term or survived certain periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 54 Geo. III c.156 extended time for unpublished works from 14 to 28 years and provided that if the author was living at term expiration he should receive profits for the residue of his life; personal representatives could have an additional 14-year term in certain cases. Practical effect depends on dates of publication and whether the earlier term had already expired before later statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Places/territorial scope of protection
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute names the places of protection: the United Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland, the Isles of Man, Jersey, and Guernsey, and every other part of the British dominions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Territorial scope is statutory; protection applies within enumerated territories. Treaties or later statutes may alter scope in other contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entry at Stationers' Hall (formal requirement and effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: An entry of the title page of each book must be made at Stationers' Hall under penalties for neglect, but such entry is not absolutely necessary to give property in the work or to sustain an action at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal entry is required by statute for certain purposes and penalties apply for neglect, but lack of entry does not prevent an initial publisher from bringing an infringement action; entry has procedural/registry significance but is not the sole basis of property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'book' (what counts as a book for copyright)
rubrics_metrics.description: A literary production need not be a multi-sheet bound volume to be a 'book' under the statute; it may be printed only on one sheet (e.g., words of a song or accompanying music); every distinct and independent part of a work may also be a 'book'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts construe 'book' broadly to include single-sheet works, individual tales or musical pieces bound with others, horn-books, rolls, etc.; the physical form or volume size is not dispositive of statutory protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printer/publisher/time statements; author's name not required
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute the name of the printer and publisher must be printed on every book; it is not necessary that the author's name appear to secure statutory rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice the publisher's imprint and date are often required for specific statutory provisions (and for pieces of music and engravings), but omission of the author's name does not defeat an author's claim to copyright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of obscenity, immorality, and libel on copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: There cannot be a copyright in any work the tendency of which is obscene or immoral; courts will not grant an injunction to protect a work offensive to public morals, nor support copyright in a work that is a libel on an individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both courts of common law and equity refuse protection where the work is obscene, immoral, or libellous. If the tendency is doubtful, a court of equity will still refrain from granting injunctive relief. Translation of an immoral work also denied protection. Exception: an author who repents and seeks to suppress his own previous immoral work may in some circumstances obtain an injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of libellous works in damages assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: If a work is a libel upon persons introduced into it, the law will not consider it valuable as a picture or literary property; damages should be assessed as the value of the physical materials (canvas and paint), not as artistic or literary value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may refuse to treat a libellous work as having property value beyond its material components; this affects remedies and damages in torts involving libellous compositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of piracy / what amounts to piracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The identity of literary works consists entirely in the sentiments and language: the same conceptions clothed in the same words are the same composition. A transcript of nearly all the sentiments and language is a glaring piracy; copying part verbatim or imitation of principal ideas can be illegal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Piracy occurs when the new work is in substance a copy — servile copying of principal parts or unfair variation qualifies. Courts examine sentiments and language, not merely form. A material alteration that is a melioration may avoid piracy; if the main design is not copied, mere presence of some shared matter is not necessarily piracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of form/manner and 'melioration' in piracy analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A variance in form and manner may be a variance in substance; a material alteration that is an improvement (melioration) cannot be considered piracy, whereas servile copying of principal parts or unfair variation is piracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges consider whether differences are substantial in substance, not just superficial changes. The central inquiry is whether the main design/principal parts have been copied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations: quantity, manner, and 'animus furandi' (intent to pirate)
rubrics_metrics.description: In judging the fairness of a quotation, the quantity taken and the manner of adoption must be considered. If the complained-of work is in substance a copy, intention need not be shown; but if only a small portion is quoted, it becomes necessary to prove anima furandi — intention to deprive the author of reward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When only small extracts are used, courts ask whether they were used fairly for purposes like advancement of science or commentary, or whether they were colorably introduced to sell a cheaper work. The question often becomes a matter of fact for a jury. Extensive verbatim copying makes intent apparent and unnecessary to prove.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of prior publication beyond statutory term
rubrics_metrics.description: If a work was published more than twenty-eight years before the 54 Geo. III act, the author is not entitled to copyright for the remainder of his lifetime; the act extended existing rights but did not re-create any expired right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If third parties published the work during the lapse between expiration of a prior statutory term and enactment of a later act, the author cannot later reclaim exclusive rights. Courts look to the timing of publication relative to statutory terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of medium/format change on rights (new work vs same work)
rubrics_metrics.description: A book originally printed in letterpress — later reproduced with high roads on copper plates and cross roads in letterpress — resulted in an injunction restraining second publication in letterpress but not extending to delineations on copper plates, which were considered a new work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing the medium or rendering (e.g., engraving vs letterpress) can produce sufficiently different expressions to be treated as a new work; courts consider whether the new presentation embodies the same sentiments and language or is materially different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments, resulting terms, and rights of assignees and personal representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: An author who sells his work generally (without limitations) has no resulting right against his own assignee after the statutory term expires. Distinctions arise between general assignments and limited (term-only) assignments: assignees of general assignments enjoy ensuing resulting terms; if an author assigns only for the first term and dies within that term, personal representatives may have a further term of 14 years without prejudice to the assignee's sale during the first term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The nature of the assignment (general vs limited) and the timing of the author's death relative to statutory periods determine whether resulting or residual terms vest in assignees or the author's estate. Courts must carefully apply the statute's language (e.g., 8 Anne and 54 Geo. III) to the facts of assignment and survivorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript protection and authors' control prior to publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary compositions in manuscript are the private and exclusive property of the author; authors have complete control over manuscripts and the right of first publishing them. Manuscripts taken from an author may give rise to trover, detinue, or trespass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity protects manuscripts against unauthorized printing; examples include injunctions where precedents or notes were stolen and printed. Manuscript publication or circulation affects the computation of statutory terms but does not necessarily forfeit copyright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript publication and calculation of statutory term
rubrics_metrics.description: If an author publishes in manuscript before printing, the words 'printed and published' in the statutes refer to the date from which the author's exercise of the right is to be dated; prior manuscript publication only varies the period from which statutory terms (e.g., 28 years) are calculated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selling or circulating a work in manuscript does not destroy statutory protection; courts have held that authors do not lose copyright by selling a composition in manuscript prior to printing, and statutory terms run from the relevant date of publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscripts performed (plays) retain copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity has held that a copyright exists in the manuscript of a play even after performance at a theatre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance does not automatically forfeit manuscript copyright; equitable remedies may be available to prevent unauthorized publication even post-performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters as literary works: classification and publication rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters can form a literary work when the form of letters is used as a literary device or when a large collection of letters from a notable writer attains literary character; the mere recipient of letters does not acquire the right to publish them by virtue of receipt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts distinguish: (1) letters written in 'letter form' as part of a literary composition (protected); (2) letters that, when collected, form a literary work (protected); and (3) ordinary private or business letters not intended for publication (not copyright works). Equity may enjoin publication of private letters on grounds of contract, confidence, or misuse, but not on copyright grounds alone unless they amount to a literary composition.
